items.readable_text:
Content:
How do we plot the graph of [MATH: y = \arccos x?] As usual, we can use a table of known values.

Content:
In order to determine these known values, let's first look at the graph of the cosine function.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/48a7ad6c06b10ff815b32ba0ab1b48fd]

Content:
The cosine function is a one-to-one function on the interval [MATH: x\in\left[ 0, \pi \right].] So if we restrict the domain to this interval, we can define the inverse function [MATH: y=\arccos x.]

Content:
Remember that the inverse swaps the domain and range of the original function. So the domain of [MATH: y=\arccos x] is [MATH: x\in[-1,1],] while the range is [MATH: y \in\left[ 0, \pi \right].] In the domain, we create a table of values:

Content:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}] | [MATH: -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}] | [MATH: -\dfrac{1}{2}] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \dfrac{1} 2] | [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt{2}} 2] | [MATH: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}} 2] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \arccos x] | [MATH: \pi] | [MATH: \dfrac{5\pi} 6] | [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi} 4] | [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi} 3] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi} 2] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi} 3] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi} 4] | [MATH: \dfrac{\pi} 6] | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
Now we can use this table to plot the graph of [MATH: y=\arccos x\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:

Content:
Some key characteristics of the graph are:

Content:
- The domain of the function is [MATH: x\in [-1, 1].]
- The range of the function is [MATH: y\in \left[ 0, \pi\right].]
- The minimum value [MATH: y=0] occurs at [MATH: x=1.]
- The maximum value [MATH: y=\pi] occurs at [MATH: x=-1.]
- The [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: y=\dfrac \pi 2.]
- The function is strictly decreasing on its entire domain.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order for a point [MATH: (a,b)] to lie on the graph of the function [MATH: y=\arccos x,] the following conditions must hold:

  • The reflected point [MATH: (b,a)] must lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\cos x.]

  • The [MATH: y]-value of the point must lie in the range of [MATH: y=\arccos x,] which is [MATH: y\in \left[ 0, \pi \right].]

With this in mind, let's check each of the points.

  • First, we consider the point [MATH: \left(-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\cos x.] [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arccos x.]

  • Next, we consider the point [MATH: \left(0,-\dfrac\pi 2 \right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(-\dfrac\pi 2,0\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\cos x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arccos x] is [MATH: y\in \left[0, \pi\right],] and [MATH: y=-\dfrac\pi 2] does not lie within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(0,-\dfrac\pi 2\right)] does not lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arccos x.]

  • Finally, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).] We note the following:

    • The point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right)] lies on the graph of [MATH: y=\cos x.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    • The range of [MATH: y=\arccos x] is [MATH: y\in \left[0, \pi\right],] and [MATH: y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] lies within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

    Therefore, the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)] does lie on the graph of [MATH: y=\arccos x.]

- Finally, we consider the point [MATH: \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right).] We note the following:

- The range of [MATH: y=\arccos x] is [MATH: y\in \left[0, \pi\right],] and [MATH: y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}] lies within this range. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
